idiom_name: public methods taking lock/Monitor or System.Threading.Lock + private implementation methods
implementation_notes: The CLR monitor - both the classic Monitor.Enter/Exit pair behind the lock statement and the newer System.Threading.Lock with EnterScope - is reentrant, so a component that calls its own public methods does not self-deadlock; the deadlock half of the pattern is already absorbed by the language and what remains is the discipline of locking once per component entry and keeping the critical section explicit. The realization is a public method whose body is the lock plus a call to a private implementation method that assumes the gate is held, so hold counts stay at 1; a callback that re-enters a public method is still a live deadlock risk precisely because reentrancy silently succeeds. When the state can be modelled with Interlocked, ConcurrentDictionary, ImmutableArray or a single-threaded owning loop, that simpler local idiom replaces the split entirely; keep the classic lock-plus-impl form where several mutations must stay atomic within one public call.
pitfalls: Reentrancy hides violations: an implementation method that calls a public method simply bumps the hold count (or re-enters Lock), so the mistake surfaces as a long critical section or inconsistent state, not as a deadlock.
Locking on this, typeof(T), a string or another shared object exposes the monitor; use a dedicated private reference object or a System.Threading.Lock field.

await is a compile error inside lock, and Task.Wait()/Result inside it can deadlock the thread pool - asynchronous critical sections belong to SemaphoreSlim.WaitAsync, a Channel or a single-threaded owner instead.

System.Threading.Lock cannot be cast to object without falling back to monitor-based locking (the compiler warns), and mixing Lock with Monitor on one instance gives two independent exclusion mechanisms.
